sources.locator: §1.6 'Countable and uncountable sets', printed pp. 16-19 (read in full); §2.3 'Real numbers: algebraic properties', printed pp. 24-26 (Theorem 2.5 and the following paragraph); §2.6, printed pp. 30-31 (Theorem 2.19); §2.8 'Density of the Rationals', printed pp. 35-36 (Lemma 2.30 and Theorem 2.31). contents.name: §1.6 Definition 1.41: finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable; the disjoint size classes and the convention that countable includes finite

§1.6 Example 1.43: the set of squares S = {n²} is countably infinite via n ↦ n², so ℕ is in bijection with a proper subset; the paragraph adds that (with choice) a set is infinite exactly when it is equinumerous with a proper subset
contents.reason: The proper-subset phenomenon is built as the one-point-deletion item; the squaring witness itself is not reproduced, because the shift φ_n already proves the sharper one-point statement, which subsumes the example.

contents.name: §1.6 Proposition 1.44: a non-empty set X is countable if and only if there is an onto map f : ℕ → X, with the recursive discarding of repeated values and the finite case f(k) = x past the list
§1.6 Proposition 1.45: ℕ × ℕ is countably infinite, by the diagonal listing (m,n) ordered by m + n and then n
§1.6 Theorem 1.46: a countable union of countable sets is countable, proved by choosing one onto f_n : ℕ → X_n for every n
contents.reason: Hunter's proof selects f_n for each n without flagging it; the library's theorem states the Axiom of Countable Choice as an explicit hypothesis and spends it at exactly that step.

contents.name: §1.6 Theorem 1.47: the power set P(ℕ) is uncountable, with the diagonal set A = {n : n ∉ A_n}
contents.reason: The general theorem is published on the A page; its instantiation at ℕ is built in this batch as ex-power-set-of-the-naturals-is-uncountable.

contents.name: §1.6 Corollary 1.48 and the binary-sequence discussion: the set Σ of binary sequences is in one-to-one correspondence with P(ℕ) and is uncountable
§1.6 Hypothesis 1.49: the continuum hypothesis and the independence results of Gödel and Cohen
§2.3 Theorem 2.5: the rational numbers are countably infinite, via the onto map g(p,q) = p/q from ℕ × ℕ onto ℚ⁺ and the embedding of ℤ
§2.3 paragraph after Theorem 2.5: since ℝ is uncountable there are many 'more' irrational numbers than rational numbers
§2.6 Theorem 2.19: the real numbers are uncountable, by Cantor's original 1874 nested-interval argument
§2.8 Lemma 2.30 and Theorem 2.31: between any two distinct reals there is a rational number (density of ℚ in ℝ), proved from the Archimedean property
§2.8 closing sentence of the section: repeated application shows there are infinitely many rational numbers between any two distinct reals

PDF pages 18-20, 30-32, 41-43 and 46-48.

contents.name: §0.3 Definition 0.3.28 and Definition 0.3.29: cardinality comparison |A| ≤ |B|, countably infinite, countable, uncountable

§0.3 Example 0.3.30: the even natural numbers have the same cardinality as ℕ, via n ↦ 2n; the paragraph after Definition 0.3.29 states (without proof) that a set is infinite if and only if it is in one-to-one correspondence with a proper subset of itself
contents.reason: The item proves the one-point-deletion form of the phenomenon in ZF and records the finite-set contrast; the doubling witness is an instance and is not rebuilt separately.

contents.name: §0.3 Example 0.3.31: ℕ × ℕ is countably infinite, listed along successive anti-diagonals
§0.3 Example 0.3.32: the rational numbers are countable, listing the fractions and leaving out fractions that have already appeared, with 0 and the negatives included
§0.3 Definition 0.3.33: the power set of a set
§0.3 Theorem 0.3.34 (Cantor) and the paragraph after it: there is no surjection A → P(A), so P(ℕ) is uncountable and ℕ, P(ℕ), P(P(ℕ)), ... are successively larger
§0.3 Exercise 0.3.24(a): if A ⊂ B and B is countably infinite then A is countable, by constructing a bijection
§0.3 Exercise 0.3.25 (challenging): if S contains a countably infinite subset then there is a countably infinite A ⊆ S with a bijection S \ A → S
contents.reason: This is the general infinite-set Dedekind argument; it needs a supplied countably infinite subset and infinite-set enumeration machinery that this pair does not build, and it is not used by any item here.

contents.name: §1.2 Theorem 1.2.4(i): the Archimedean property of ℝ
§1.2 Theorem 1.2.4(ii): ℚ is dense in ℝ, together with the preceding sentence that any interval contains infinitely many rationals
§1.4 Theorem 1.4.2 (Cantor): ℝ is uncountable, by Cantor's 1874 nested-interval proof, stated as a direct construction that every countably infinite subset misses some point
§1.4 paragraph after Theorem 1.4.2: there are a lot more irrational numbers than rational numbers; ℚ is countable and ℝ is uncountable
§1.5 Theorem 1.5.2 (Cantor): (0,1] is uncountable, by the decimal diagonal argument
contents.reason: The library proves every nondegenerate interval uncountable by the 1874 nested-interval route; the decimal-digit route rests on decimal expansions, which are not constructed at this order, so it is not reproduced.

contents.name: §1.5 Exercise 1.5.5: using binary expansions, the cardinality of ℝ equals that of P(ℕ)
contents.reason: The identification ℝ ≈ P(ℕ) needs binary expansions and the completeness machinery of Chapter 1; the binary-sequence space itself is built as ex-binary-sequences-are-uncountable, without the identification with ℝ.
